How Sinch modernized its enterprise data warehouse from Snowflake to BigQuery to power AI

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (937 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, as the scale of global communications grows larger and larger, enterprise platforms must process billions of interactions with customers across a complex network of touchpoints without breaking them.
  • Managing massive international messaging traffic brings significant architectural challenges, so Sinch built a distributed, multi-cloud data footprint across AWS and GCP, with separate Snowflake instances running in the EU, US, and Australia.
  • Here’s how we engineered Sinch’s new, modern, cost-efficient, and AI-ready platform architecture.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

According to recent reports, as the scale of global communications grows larger and larger, enterprise platforms must process billions of interactions with customers across a complex network of touchpoints without breaking them. A prime example is Sinch, one of the world’s leading cloud communications and customer engagement (CPaaS) companies, which processes billions of customer interactions, SMS routing events, voice calls, and transactional messages.

Managing massive international messaging traffic brings significant architectural challenges, so Sinch built a distributed, multi-cloud data footprint across AWS and GCP, with separate Snowflake instances running in the EU, US, and Australia. To eliminate data silos, curb monthly billing spikes, establish a single governed source of truth, and unlock the next generation of predictive AI capabilities, Sinch partnered with Google Cloud Professional Services to migrate its enterprise data warehouse to Google BigQuery.

Here’s how we engineered Sinch’s new, modern, cost-efficient, and AI-ready platform architecture.

Before it embarked on this modernization journey, Sinch faced several architectural and operational friction points:.

Cross-regional data sprawl: The company’s separate Snowflake instances in the EU, US, and Australia required intricate inter-region replication, which caused  multi-directional dependencies and complex cross-warehouse data management.

Resource spikes and commercial inefficiencies: Heavy monthly billing runs drove severe compute spikes in the US, even as other regions had underutilized capacity.

It has been revealed that high-volume scanning vs. dialect disparities: A single US email event table could generate up to 100 TB of daily scans. Meanwhile, mission-critical SQL relied on Snowflake-specific concurrency and table-swapping paradigms for concurrency validation, which lacked 1:1 equivalents in cloud-native SQL.

Recent findings suggest that “Google Cloud's engineering expertise helped us overcome several technical challenges during our migration, particularly around optimising Spark partitioning and restructuring incremental data loads. This allowed us to identify more efficient approaches, improve performance and ensure we built a scalable, reliable solution for the future.”Dan Peters, senior manager, Data Delivery, Sinch.

To mitigate operational risk and prevent downtime for Sinch’s critical enterprise workloads (including ERP and NetSuite integrations), we initiated a phased migration framework:.

A use case pilot validation: The migration kicked off with a dedicated use case MVP that spanned 20 tables and 125 GB of refined data and automatically validated end-to-end data fidelity.

Layered strategy for coupled pipelines: Rather than attempting to cleanly slice interconnected business domains in the EU, the team adopted a layered approach —  migrating raw and base (bronze and silver) layers, establishing automated data ingestion, and stabilizing core entities before repointing consumption marts.

Orchestration consolidation: Sinch consolidated 36 independent ETL workflows into a single parameterized orchestrator by using Google Cloud Workflows, which streamlined CI/CD deployment logic, and reduced operational overhead.

Sources indicate that sinch transitioned its data ingestion pipelines to Dataproc Serverless (running Apache Spark 3.5), which directly pulled refined data into native BigQuery tables from S3 and Databricks Unity Catalog. And to overcome batch quota limits and resource exhaustion on billion-row datasets, Sinch optimized jobs by increasing Spark repartitioning factors to 50.

For its incremental pipelines, the team eliminated data duplication while minimizing query read costs by replacing slow, keyless merge statements with an optimized insert-and-overwrite windowing strategy.

In order to accelerate the translation of more than 1,200 dbt models across global projects, Sinch utilized Google Cloud BigQuery Migration Service alongside a set of custom AI translation skills. Here’s how:.

The team refactored Snowflake-specific table versioning and concurrency management paradigms into deterministic transaction blocks and view abstraction pointers. This ensured atomic updates and consistent data access.

According to recent reports, sinch leveraged specialized Google skills for other regional migration — specifically the dbt-sf-to-bq-translator skill powered by the underlying BigQuery Translation API — to automate the conversion of dbt models from Snowflake to BigQuery SQL syntax. This significantly reduced manual refactoring effort and error rates.

Concurrency checks that relied on row-level locking were redesigned into serialized batch validations.

Integer overflow risks in massive calculation tables were solved by adopting a tiered precision strategy (favoring NUMERIC over BIGNUMERIC), which cut storage costs and preserved absolute precision.

Industry observers note that “Migrating over a thousand complex dbt models and translating legacy SQL required a robust, automated approach. Google Cloud's guidance on query restructuring helped us streamline pipeline development and remove compilation blockers. The team shared best practices for migrating code from Snowflake to BigQuery, such as replacing Snowflake SWAP WITH and hybrid-table patterns with BigQuery time travel. They also helped us build workflows that copy data from Snowflake to BigQuery and run our dbt jobs along the way, which sped up our move to BigQuery.”Varun Gupta, Senior Data Engineer, Sinch.

By completing the migration, Sinch successfully transformed the operational bottleneck of its global data footprint into a driver of enterprise growth:.

High data churn; lengthy multi-hour batch runs.

Significantly faster query and pipeline processing speeds across billions of records.

Unpredictable month-end billing spikes.

Predictable capacity management with BigQuery reservations and slot autoscaling.

Segmented data warehouses requiring external pipelines.

Native BQML and Vertex AI decision intelligence platform.

In a recent development, with its core European warehouse workloads stabilized on BigQuery and data validation consistently outperforming legacy benchmarks, Sinch is now expanding this modern blueprint across its Australian (SMB) and US analytics. The SMB instance migration is already in progress and is utilizing Antigravity skills for the Snowflake to BigQuery translation.

By unifying data storage, operational governance, and serverless compute, Sinch has built a resilient platform that delivers real-time messaging reliability today while positioning the organization to capture the full potential of enterprise AI tomorrow.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Industry observers note that local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this upcoming generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

Here's what changed, and what's next:.

Sources indicate that the core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:.

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:.

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

According to recent reports, support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:.

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:.

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Recent findings suggest that reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

Recent findings suggest that API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:.

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:.

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Sources indicate that language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

#38369. Look Before You Commit: Visual-Evidence-Guided Decoding for Multimodal Diffusion Language Models

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • ⚡ Quick Read (146 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Look Before You Commit: Visual-Evidence-Guided Decoding for Multimodal Diffusion Language Models

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (146 words, ⚡ Quick Read) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.31677v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Diffusion multimodal large language models rely on confidence to decide when to commit candidate tokens during generation. In multimodal tasks, however, confidence cannot distinguish whether a candidate originates from image evidence or the language prior. We perform paired forward ablation and find that nearly nine out of ten high-confidence commits are insensitive to the image, while degenerate and hallucination samples exhibit significant increases in the entropy of deep-layer attention organization. Based on this diagnosis, we propose CD-APC, a training-free decoding method. CD-APC performs evidence-adjusted scoring within a base-supported pool and uses dual gating based on model acceptability and contrastive concentration to decide whether to commit, together with an inverse-window mechanism that adapts to inter-step difficulty. Across two backbones and five benchmarks, CD-APC consistently improves performance, indicating that stable visual evidence improves model outputs.

The AWS Quick web app now brings the Quick desktop experience to your browser. Create, share, and use the same agents and skills as on desktop, with the same connectors. Start each day with a daily briefing and a prioritized feed of the email and messages that need your attention. Quick keeps your conversations, agents, and files synchronized across web, desktop, and mobile, so work you start on one surface carries over to the others. Your dashboards, topics, and spaces work as before.

Industry observers note that additionally, agents you start or schedule from the web keep running after you close your browser. Schedule an agent in the morning, answer its questions from the mobile app between meetings, and review the results on your desktop. Mission Control shows what your agents have finished and where they need your input. The Quick browser extension and Microsoft 365 add-ins for Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Outlook are also updated.

It has been revealed that these updates are available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and US East (N. Virginia).

Existing Quick customers can sign in to the web app to get started, or download the desktop app here. The Quick mobile app is available for free from the Apple App Store and Google Play Store. To learn more, see the AWS Quick User Guide.

Searching for distant planets with Astra

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1441 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, two amateur astronomers used Codex and Astra to look for signs of planets in public telescope data.
  • Sources indicate that astronomers have confirmed more than 6,400 planets beyond our solar system⁠(opens in a new window) since the first ones were announced in 1992⁠(opens in a new window).
  • It has been revealed that *Data from the NASA Exoplanet Archive’s Planetary Systems Composite Parameters table⁠(opens in a latest window).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, two amateur astronomers used Codex and Astra to look for signs of planets in public telescope data. Now they’ve given professional astronomers a few places to look more closely.

Sources indicate that astronomers have confirmed more than 6,400 planets beyond our solar system⁠(opens in a new window) since the first ones were announced in 1992⁠(opens in a new window). A worldwide community of amateur astronomers has long been part of that search. Some comb through public telescope data for small, repeated dips in a star’s brightness that could signal an orbiting planet. Others use their own telescopes to watch for the next dip and share what they see with researchers.

It has been revealed that *Data from the NASA Exoplanet Archive’s Planetary Systems Composite Parameters table⁠(opens in a latest window). 2026 data are year to date through November 24, 2026.

In a recent development, astronomers have used AI in this search for years. In 2017, researchers trained a neural network on 15,000 signals from NASA’s Kepler Space Telescope⁠(opens in a new window) that astronomers had already examined. From those examples, the model learned to recognize which patterns in starlight were most likely to come from a planet. When the researchers used it to examine weaker signals, one led them to an eighth planet orbiting a star called Kepler-90⁠(opens in a new window).

It has been revealed that now, tools like Astra are helping amateur astronomers design and run searches of their own, often on data that has already yielded the more obvious exoplanet signals. Kevin Bond, an engineer at OpenAI, came to astronomy through his love of photographing the night sky. He used Codex to search observations of about 100,000 stars from the Kepler telescope, a planet-hunting mission that ran from 2009 to 2018. Ethan Byrd, founder of the email infrastructure start-up Primitive, has always loved astronomy. Working independently of Bond, he tried several AI models before choosing Astra to help him analyze telescope data from about 19 million stars.

Both searches identified potential exoplanets. Bond and Byrd have now turned to astronomers for an independent assessment of their results. Bond contacted an astronomer at the SETI Institute, who ran an independent search and found two of the same signals in the Kepler data. Byrd sent one of his strongest candidates to researchers working on NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) mission. It’s in line for further analysis, and two more candidates are awaiting submission.

One of the most common ways to find an exoplanet is to watch the star it orbits. When a planet passes in front of its star from our point of view on Earth, it blocks a tiny amount of starlight. Astronomers call that crossing a transit. On a graph of the star’s brightness over time, known as a light curve, a transit highlights up as a dip. If the dip keeps coming back at regular intervals, astronomers know when to watch for it again.

It has been revealed that searching for that pattern across thousands of stars is partly a coding problem. Astronomers have published methods for picking out faint, recurring dips in years of measurements. Bond used Codex to compare those methods, combine them in a search program, and test whether changes to the code improved the search. One AI agent scanned the light curves for promising signals. Another ran more detailed checks on the candidates the first one flagged.

According to recent reports, bond ran the program on public data from the Kepler Space Telescope. The search flagged more than 200 signals, including 10 from previously confirmed planets. Finding those known planets gave Bond confidence that the program could pick out the kinds of signals he was looking for.

Two stars stood out. The first, KIC 5689121, is a relatively cool star about half the size of our sun in the constellation Lyra. The Codex search found a dip in brightness every 13.8 days. If a planet is causing it, the amount of light it blocks suggests it could be about 2.4 times Earth’s diameter.

These four curves show the same Kepler observations aligned on a 13.77-day cycle.

Industry observers note that the second star, KIC 6691030, is faint and lies in the northern sky. The Codex search found a dip in its brightness every 4.8 days, consistent with a planet smaller than Neptune. These were the two signals the SETI Institute astronomer found independently. Confirming what caused them could take months or years.

In a recent development, byrd used Astra to design two searches. One looked broadly for exoplanet candidates. The other focused on stars’ habitable zones. A habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where a planet with a suitable atmosphere could support liquid water on its surface.

Byrd then asked Astra to review published methods, build the search software, and run initial checks on promising signals. His searches drew on observations from TESS, which NASA launched in 2018, and from other public telescope archives.

Recent findings suggest that kepler watched one field for four years. TESS surveyed both hemispheres in its first 26 sectors, from 2018 to 2020. The star field comes from NASA’s TESS mosaic through September 2025⁠(opens in a latest window), clipped to that original survey footprint. The wider gap indicates where TESS pointed farther north during six observing sectors. The inset marks KIC 5689121⁠(opens in a new window) in the original Kepler field⁠(opens in a new window). See NASA’s final prime-mission coverage maps⁠(opens in a new window) and its earlier field-of-view animation⁠(opens in a new window).

The first pass through the data turned up 49 candidates. Byrd sent one of his strongest candidates to researchers working on the TESS mission, where it is awaiting further analysis. His search is still running.

Sources indicate that when astronomers see a star dim, they have to consider what else might explain it. Two stars passing in front of one another can produce a similar dip. Even a change in temperature aboard a telescope can affect its instruments enough to make a star appear to dim.

Astronomers can use statistics to show that an exoplanet is the most likely explanation for a series of dips. They can also collect more observations, sometimes using a different method. For example, an orbiting planet’s gravity tugs on its star, causing it to move slightly toward and away from us. That motion, called radial velocity, reveals up as tiny shifts in the color of the star’s light. Astronomers then publish their findings in a peer-reviewed journal so others can examine the evidence.

Recent findings suggest that for Bond and Byrd, each candidate is a question that can be tested. If a planet is passing in front of the star in Lyra every 13.8 days, astronomers can watch for the next crossing. Further observations can help establish whether the dip repeats as expected, while additional checks can help determine what is causing it.

You can contribute without owning a telescope. NASA’s Exoplanet Watch⁠(opens in a new window) lets you request data and learn to plot a light curve yourself. Its broader exoplanet citizen science programs⁠(opens in a new window) offer other ways to participate.

It has been revealed that if you have access to a telescope, Exoplanet Watch walks users through how to collect data on transiting exoplanets and participate in observation campaigns. AAVSO’s Exoplanet Observing Program⁠(opens in a new window) can show you how to measure a dip in starlight and share your observations with the researchers studying that planet. And the Unistellar Network Investigating TESS Exoplanets⁠(opens in a new window) coordinates volunteers around the world with a certain type of telescope to observe the same star, helping astronomers catch transits that can last longer than a single night.

Industry observers note that astronomy has a long history of people around the world following their curiosity and sharing what they find. Bond and Byrd are part of that tradition. Their searches are still open, but they turned a love of the night sky into leads that other astronomers can investigate. We want more people to have that opportunity, in astronomy and across science.

If you want to follow along with latest findings, practical guidance, and perspectives from researchers using AI to advance science check out the OpenAI science blog⁠.

  • Recent findings suggest that the investment was led by Canary.
  • Canary noted it first met co-founders Edward Konig and Rafael Katalan in August 2025 and tracked their progress for over a year before investing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

IKKB, a financial management platform for companies operating across borders, has closed a $3m seed round to secure regulatory licences and develop upcoming products for its multi-currency business account.

Recent findings suggest that the investment was led by Canary. According to the announcement, the capital will help IKKB obtain the licences it needs to operate as a regulated institution in each of its markets. It will also fund further products built on top of the core account. The firm already has licensing applications under way in Brazil, the US and Canada.

Canary noted it first met co-founders Edward Konig and Rafael Katalan in August 2025 and tracked their progress for over a year before investing. The investor said the pair learned swiftly, made difficult decisions with long-term goals in mind and achieved a great deal on limited funding. Canary believes a growing number of companies now operate internationally from launch, while the financial infrastructure supporting them remains slow, costly and fragmented.

Sources indicate that IKKB’s offering has grown considerably in a short time. Just over a year ago, its product had a single function, converting PIX payments into US dollars. It has since become a multi-currency account for businesses, holding balances in BRL, USD, EUR and MXN. The account connects to local payment rails in Brazil, the US, Europe and Mexico, and offers corporate cards in BRL and USD. The team developed the platform internally on modest capital and prioritised regulatory work from the outset.

According to recent reports, the firm is focused on giving Latin American businesses a global account. Firms can manage international payments, foreign exchange and treasury from a single platform. The service operates on stablecoin rails and applies AI to provide additional services alongside the account. IKKB offers accounts, cards, currency exchange, payments and treasury management.

IKKB was founded to reduce the friction and expense of moving money across borders for both businesses and individuals. Its mission is to make international transfers as straightforward as moving funds between accounts, offering transparent FX and payments across all rails without the hidden spreads and bureaucracy associated with traditional banks.

arXiv:2611.31656v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) ranks memory chunks by semantic similarity to the query. Many methods improve on this by learning from feedback on what was retrieved, but each is a separate heuristic, with no account of when it is the right choice. We introduce BRAG, a generative model of retrieval with use. Each chunk generates the queries it answers from a mixture of von Mises-Fisher components anchored at its original embedding, and each chunk has a latent utility that drifts over time. The model gives the optimal inference, a closed-form filter that stores a few keys and two scalars per chunk and updates them online from the labels of a curator, and it frames retrieval as a control problem. It also reveals when existing methods are optimal. Query averaging, Rocchio-style feedback and frequency reranking are special cases with fixed parameters, NUDGE is the case of one key per chunk with no dynamics, and LADER the limit of one key per past query. On two public long-term memory benchmarks, BRAG matches these methods on queries asked before, as expected, because when nothing changes over time the assumptions behind these special cases hold. On harder problems, where a new chunk makes an old one obsolete, BRAG outscores them. They all stay at plain-search level (Recall@5 0.67-0.71), while BRAG retrieves the new chunk 0.80-0.86 of the time. We also ran BRAG on three of NUDGE's seven text benchmarks, and it matches or beats NUDGE on all three. On nine months of a personal agent's memory (20,640 chunks), BRAG raises Recall@5 on held-out queries from 0.75 to 0.98 and Recall@1 from 0.44 to 0.97, with little change on chunks never queried.

#38364. GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

GPT-6 models demonstrate intrinsic protein-design capabilities

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4223 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Our GPT‑6 family of models can design newly introduced protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.
  • An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks.
  • Recent findings suggest that in lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs indicated evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our GPT‑6 family of models can design newly introduced protein shapes and the sequence of their chemical building blocks using only reasoning and code, without calling specialized biology models to generate those designs.

An internal research model matched or outperformed specialized models on many protein design tasks. Researchers could also guide designs by prompting the model on where a protein should attach and what shape it should take.

Recent findings suggest that in lab tests with Onava, proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs indicated evidence of binding, or attachment, across five targets. Redesigned antibodies also retained binding. Specialized models helped supply sequences and select candidates for testing.

The models’ written reasoning and code suggest they draw on math, physics, chemistry, and biological knowledge to reason about protein shapes and interactions with other molecules.

In a preprint titled GPT‑6 as a Universal Foundation Model for Protein Biology: Beyond Specialized Models, we show that our GPT‑6 family of models has intrinsic capabilities for designing latest proteins: the models can design new protein structures and sequences without relying on specialized biology models, using only reasoning and general-purpose coding tools.

Proteins do much of the work in living cells. They drive the chemical reactions that sustain life, carry oxygen through the blood, and defend the body against infection. Incorrectly shaped proteins can also cause disease and dysfunction. Proteins are made from chains of chemical building blocks called amino acids. The order, or sequence, of these amino acids helps determine how a protein folds into a three-dimensional shape, which in turn influences what it does.

Scientists often start with a clear idea of what they want a protein to do. They might want it to block a signal that helps cancer cells evade the immune system or to help capture carbon dioxide from the air. The challenge is to work out what three-dimensional structure would enable the protein to do its job and which amino acid sequence would give it that structure. Specialized biology models capable of generating three-dimensional protein structures and sequences have made this work more practical.

Using and coordinating these specialized models requires substantial expertise. Each accepts particular kinds of inputs and constraints, and these models cannot easily accept new kinds of information without changes to their software or additional training. In contrast, a general-purpose model capable of performing the work of multiple specialized models can easily adapt to new instructions and requirements.

Industry observers note that our research illustrates the potential power of pairing natural language with intrinsic protein capabilities. We could guide our models at scales ranging from a single bond between two atoms to the overall shape of a protein. For example, we asked GPT‑6.2 to predict where and how a small molecule would bind to a protein. When we already knew which two atoms formed a bond, we could give the model that information and ask how the rest of the molecule would fit. We could switch between these tasks simply by changing the prompt, without retraining the model. We also asked our models to design small proteins called minibinders and marked where each should attach to its target, and further specified how many coils or strands each minibinder should contain. An internal model followed that instruction with near-perfect fidelity in its three-dimensional designs.

Industry observers note that points farther from the center indicate better performance. Newer generations of models improved on many of the 14 protein tasks tested.

According to recent reports, we ran computational tests of whether the GPT‑6 models series could design small proteins to bind given targets, build proteins around specified structural features, predict protein structures and molecular interactions, and rank how sequence changes affect properties such as stability and binding. Our latest models performed comparably to or better than specialized models on most tasks, although predicting a complete protein structure remained a clear weakness.

Recent findings suggest that the models’ written reasoning and code offer clues to how they approach these tasks. They draw on mathematics, physics, chemistry, and coding alongside knowledge of recurring patterns in protein sequences and structures. For example, when designing a small protein intended to bind to IL-7Rα, the model proposed how the two proteins might interact, then wrote and executed code to explore different protein shapes and amino acid choices that could support that interaction.

Sources indicate that the model’s written reasoning and code show it drawing on math, physics, chemistry and biology to design a protein intended to attach to IL-7Rα. It examines the target’s surface, arranges five coiled sections into a protein shape, and checks how the two proteins could fit together.

Sources indicate that with our research partner, Onava⁠(opens in a new window), we also tested the models’ structure and sequence designs in the lab. First, Onava made small proteins based on three-dimensional structures designed by a pre-released version of GPT‑6.2. Specialized models supplied amino acid sequences and helped select candidates for testing. For each of the five targets we chose, at least one protein showed evidence of binding in the lab. In separate experiments, GPT‑6.2 designed new amino acid sequences for existing minibinders and antibodies. Following candidate selection with specialized models, many of the redesigned proteins also showed evidence of binding to the same targets as the originals.

Recent findings suggest that our first laboratory experiment tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design small proteins that would bind to their intended targets. We compared computational measurements of quality against RFdiffusion, a specialized model for protein design, and found that GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs scored slightly lower while our latest internal models scored higher. For the lab experiment, we made proteins based on GPT‑6.2’s designs and measured how strongly they bound to their targets.

We gave GPT‑6.2 the three-dimensional structures of five target proteins and marked where we wanted a minibinder to attach. It then wrote code to create three-dimensional designs for potential minibinders, without using specialized protein AI models.

To turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins we could test in the lab, we needed amino acid sequences that would fold into the proposed structures. We used a specialized AI model called SolubleMPNN to suggest sequences for each design. Other specialized protein models helped us select candidates predicted to fold as designed and bind at the intended site on the target.

GPT‑6.2 designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to chosen targets. Specialized models then proposed amino acid sequences—the order of the proteins’ chemical building blocks—and helped select designs for our research partner Onava to make and test in the lab.

Sources indicate that we tested 322 minibinders against 5 targets in the lab. Of those, 35 (10.9%) tested positive for binding to their intended target. We found 5 hits for PD-L1 (a protein some cancers use to evade the immune system), 3 for IL-7Rα, 1 for TrkA, 8 for VEGF-A and 18 for IL-17A. The original RFdiffusion study⁠(opens in a latest window) reported higher hit rates, but rates depend heavily on how strictly researchers filter designs before lab validation and their definition of binding. Nevertheless, our results provide early evidence that we can turn GPT‑6.2’s three-dimensional designs into proteins that bind to their intended targets in the lab.

An internal research model designed shapes for small proteins intended to attach to the target proteins shown in gray. The colored shapes compare each design with a computational prediction of how the protein would fold and fit against its target.

We tested whether GPT‑6.2 could design the sequences itself. We gave it three-dimensional models of how existing minibinders fit against their targets, withheld the original amino acid sequences, and asked it to propose latest ones. Specialized models helped us choose which proteins to make and test in the lab.

It has been revealed that for three targets, we started with computationally predicted structures of confirmed minibinders whose sequences Onava had collected from earlier studies. In our initial lab screens, we saw binding in 75 of 88 designs for MDM2 (85%), 26 of 42 for VEGF-A (62%), and 8 of 59 for PD-1 (14%). The amino acid sequences proposed by GPT‑6.2 also often differed significantly from the original minibinder sequences, with a median of 50% for VEGF-A, 43% for MDM2, and 15% for PD-1.

Recent findings suggest that we also asked GPT‑6.2 to design upcoming sequences for three unpublished minibinder shapes it had generated earlier: two targeting PD-L1 and one targeting IL-7Rα. A specialized model, ProteinMPNN, had already supplied one sequence for each shape, and proteins made from those sequences had shown binding in the lab. Of the 107 proteins made from GPT‑6.2’s new sequences, 14 (13.1%) demonstrated binding.

Given an unpublished structure, GPT‑6.2 had come up with two substantially different sequences that both highlighted signs of binding to the same target. For the same PD-L1 minibinder structure, GPT‑6.2 designed two sequences different from the original in 52 and 58 out of 90 total amino acids. The two also differed from each other at 44 positions, nearly half the sequence.

The unpublished structures and substantial differences in sequence give us strong evidence that GPT‑6.2’s capabilities extend beyond memorization. The results also suggest we could use GPT‑6.2 to intrinsically design both a minibinder’s structure and its sequence.

According to recent reports, researchers often redesign an antibody’s binding loops to help it grip its target more tightly, a process called affinity maturation. They may also want it to bind more selectively, so it’s less likely to attach to similar proteins. We tested a first step toward those goals by asking our models to design fresh loop sequences that preserved binding to the original target.

Recent findings suggest that we started with six small antibodies (VHHs) that bind to the same protein, IL-4Rα. For each antibody, we gave GPT‑6.2 its predicted three-dimensional structure and most of its amino acid sequence, leaving out the three loops that help the antibody grip its target. We asked the model to design upcoming sequences for them. Of the 182 designs we tested, 128 (70%) showed signs of binding to IL-4Rα.

According to recent reports, we then tested how precisely we could guide the model’s changes to existing therapeutic antibodies. This time, we gave the model the original sequences and asked it to change about half the amino acids in each of three binding loops while keeping the rest of the sequence intact. We tested the redesigned portions of the antibodies as fragments in the lab. Of 272 fragments based on five therapeutic antibodies, 179 (66%) demonstrated binding to the original target, PD-1 or PD-L1.

A long-term goal of programmable structure-based design is to let researchers specify structural constraints in natural language. In our computational evaluations, our models consistently designed minibinders that contacted the required locations on the target. We could also specify the minibinder’s structural class (all helices, all strands, or a combination) and control the number of coils and strands with near-perfect fidelity. The same approach lets us express more detailed requirements for the binding interface, such as which target amino acids should be buried upon binding or whether the minibinder and target should interact through specific interactions such as “β-sheet–β-sheet”. As our model’s reasoning capabilities improve, we envision researchers guiding protein structure generation much as they guide image generation today, by describing the features they want.

Our model was asked to design small proteins with specified shapes: mainly coils (orange), mainly strands (blue), or a mix. Some instructions also specified how many coils or strands to include. The designs are intended to attach to PD-L1 or PD-1, shown in gray.

In a recent development, most enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions. When designing a latest enzyme, researchers may know how a few key amino acids need to be arranged at the site where the reaction happens. Those amino acids can lie far apart along the protein chain. The challenge is to design the rest of the protein so that, as the chain folds, it brings them together and holds them in place.

Industry observers note that we tested our models on 30 challenges from MotifBench⁠(opens in a fresh window), including examples drawn from enzymes and from sites where proteins bind to one another. We gave the models a specific three-dimensional arrangement of amino acids, called a motif, and asked them to use coding tools to design the rest of the protein around it. This task is called motif scaffolding.

Industry observers note that for each design, we used ProteinMPNN to propose eight possible amino acid sequences, and ESMFold⁠(opens in a new window) to predict how each would fold. We counted the design as a success if at least one predicted structure both preserved the motif and closely matched the overall structure the model had designed.

In a preliminary analysis, 43.7% of the designs we evaluated from our latest internal model met both criteria, compared with 27.8% for RFdiffusion. While laboratory experiments are needed to find out whether these proteins could carry out the intended function, such as speeding up a particular reaction, this provides strong computational evidence of our models’ intrinsic protein capabilities.

An internal research model designed protein structures around a small region whose shape had to stay fixed, shown in gold. The colored shapes compare the model’s designs with computer predictions of how the proteins would fold. Panels showing only gold had no design that passed the computer checks.

Sources indicate that in motif scaffolding, we specified how a few amino acids should sit relative to one another. We then determined whether we could also guide the design of an entire protein by specifying its overall fold. We gave our models a chain length and a code from CATH⁠(opens in a latest window), a system scientists use to classify protein structures. The models then had to work out where each amino acid should go in three-dimensional space.

According to recent reports, many designs captured the broad layout we asked for. The harder part was getting the chain to follow the right path through it. Two proteins can have several coiled stretches packed together in a similar bundle, for example, yet differ in the order in which the chain connects them.

We counted a design as a success if at least one amino acid sequence was predicted to adopt the requested fold and closely match the model’s three-dimensional design. Across 200 challenges, 18.9% of the designs we evaluated from our latest internal model passed, compared with 17.1% for Proteina, a specialized protein design model.

An internal research model was asked to design proteins with specified overall shapes, such as bundles of coils or layers of strands. The colored shapes compare selected designs with computer predictions of how they would fold, showing examples where the two closely match.

Recent findings suggest that many medicines, including aspirin, are small molecules, chemical compounds much smaller than the proteins they act on. Predicting where a small molecule binds to a protein and how it fits there is called docking. These predictions can help researchers decide how to modify a drug candidate so it binds more tightly to its target. To test our models, we started with experimentally determined structures of small molecules bound to proteins. We digitally removed each small molecule and gave the models the protein structure along with a text description of how the molecule’s atoms were connected (a sequence of characters called SMILES). We then asked the models to predict where the molecule had been bound and how it was oriented.

It has been revealed that for our first docking test, we used the PoseBusters dataset⁠(opens in a new window), a collection of three-dimensional structures that show how small molecules bind to proteins. Researchers determined these structures experimentally, giving us a way to check the models’ predictions. Without being told where on the protein each molecule had bound, the models had to predict both where the molecule fit and which way it faced. GPT‑6.2 closely matched the molecule’s observed position and orientation in 93% of scored predictions, compared with 96% for our latest internal model and 50% for DiffDock-L, a specialized docking model.

Sources indicate that in practice, researchers may already know something about how a molecule binds. One major advantage of a GPT model is that we can give additional information directly in the prompt. We tested this on 179 structures from the Scarpino dataset⁠(opens in a latest window), where each protein structure forms a chemical bond with a small molecule, tethering the two together. We told our models which two atoms formed the bond and asked them to predict how the rest of the molecule fit against the protein. GPT‑6.2 closely matched the experimental structure in 92% of scored predictions⁠(opens in a new window), and our latest internal model did so in 97%, while DiffDock⁠(opens in a new window) reached 60%.

An internal research model predicted where and how small molecules would fit against proteins, shown in gray. Purple shows the model’s predictions, and teal shows the molecules’ positions determined in earlier experiments. In these examples, the predictions closely match the experimental structures.

Recent findings suggest that where an antibody binds can help explain whether it blocks another protein from attaching to the same site. We tested how accurately successive generations of GPT could predict where an antibody binds and which way it faces. For hundreds of pairs of antibodies and targets, we showed the models the two proteins separately and hid some of the atomic detail (all side chains) on their surfaces.

With the side-chain details hidden, the mean DockQ score (a commonly used metric in which higher values indicate a closer match to the experimentally observed arrangement) increased from approximately 0.05 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.28 for GPT‑6, 0.57 for GPT‑6.2, and 0.81 for our latest internal model, at each model’s highest evaluated compute setting.

Because these structures were public, the models may have seen the same antibody-target pairs or similar ones during training. Even so, each generation of our models predicted more accurately how the two proteins fit together, even with all side-chain positions hidden. That progress gives us reason to be optimistic about harder docking problems.

In a recent development, each row compares four models’ predictions of how an antibody attaches to its target protein. Colored shapes show the model’s prediction; dark gray shows the position observed in experiments. Results improved with each successive generation of model.

We can design far more proteins on a computer than we can make and test in the lab. Even after we settle on a promising structure, we may have many amino acid sequences to choose from. We tested whether our models could help researchers decide which versions to make first by predicting how changes to a protein’s sequence would affect its stability, activity, or ability to bind to a target.

Sources indicate that we drew on four public datasets from experiments in which scientists had replaced one or more amino acids in a protein and measured the effects. For each test, we gave our models the sequence of the protein the scientists started with and the sequences of 50 modified versions. We told the models what the scientists had measured, withheld the results, and asked them to rank the 50 versions without using coding tools, by reasoning only.

In a recent development, in one study of protein stability, we asked the models to rank 50 versions of a protein by how likely each was to be folded at room temperature. We compared the predicted order with the order observed in the lab using a measure called rank correlation. A value of 1 means the rankings match perfectly, 0 means there’s no consistent relationship, and −1 means the order is exactly reversed. Across 265 sets from the stability study, each model generation improved, from 0.41 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.52 for GPT‑6, 0.57 for GPT‑6.2, and 0.66 for our latest internal model.

In each of the four datasets, GPT‑6.2 and our latest internal model produced more accurate rankings on average than ESM2-650M, a specialized protein model.

Earlier, we relied on specialized models to predict whether an amino acid sequence would fold into the structure our models had designed. We wanted to see how close our models are to making that prediction themselves. We gave our models the amino acid sequences of proteins with known three-dimensional structures. Using only basic coding tools, the models predicted how each chain would fold in three dimensions. We evaluated their predictions using a measure called TM-score. A score of 1 means a perfect match to the real structure, and scores above 0.5 generally indicate that the prediction captures the overall fold.

In a recent development, the biggest gains are visible in individual examples. For some proteins, our latest internal model closely reproduced folds that earlier models missed. Across the full test, the average score rose from 0.16 for GPT‑5.6 to 0.26 for GPT‑6.2 and 0.38 for our latest internal model. The specialized model ESMFold2 averaged 0.93, so there’s still a substantial gap in how reliably our models can predict a whole protein’s structure from its sequence alone.

Sources indicate that what if researchers already know most of the structure and want to fill in a missing piece? We tested this on 100 antibody fragments. For each one, we gave our models the amino acid sequences and the surrounding three-dimension structure, hiding the six loops that help the antibody recognize its target. Our latest internal model often predicted both the shape and position of those loops quite accurately. ESMFold2 was still more accurate overall, even working from the sequences alone.

Each model was given the same protein sequence—the order of its chemical building blocks—and asked to predict its 3D shape. The colored shapes show the predictions, and dark gray shows the structure measured in experiments.

Industry observers note that each model was given a partial structure and tasked with predicting the missing regions corresponding to the antibody CDRs. The colored regions show predictions from the internal model and ESMFold2 compared with the experimentally determined structures.

It is vital to note that our protein design campaign relied on specialized structure prediction models such as Boltz-2, OpenDDE, and ESMFold2 to filter candidates. Our results show that GPT models have intrinsic capabilities comparable to specialized models at two stages of the workflow: backbone generation, where researchers commonly use RFdiffusion; and sequence redesign, where they commonly use ProteinMPNN. Our results therefore do not yet establish that our models can generate de novo minibinders end-to-end in a zero-shot setting without help from specialized models.

According to recent reports, our work demonstrates yet again the jagged capability frontier. Predicting a complete protein structure from its amino acid sequence remains substantially harder for our models than several of the component tasks above. On that task, even our best internal models remained well behind specialized structure-prediction models.

According to recent reports, some benchmark results also require careful interpretation. In tests that asked models to infer amino acid sequences from protein structures, unusually high accuracy may partly reflect memorization or patterns left by the process used to generate those structures. Those results alone do not establish reliable performance on unfamiliar proteins.

According to recent reports, the laboratory results provide a more direct test of whether proposed designs can work, but binding is only one step toward a useful research tool or medicine. Further work would need to establish properties such as specificity, stability, and biological activity, along with safety and efficacy for therapeutic applications.

Recent findings suggest that this work is an early step toward programmable molecular design at OpenAI. Our goal is to let scientists describe what they want a molecule to do in plain language and use our models to help design candidates to test in the lab. To make that approach useful for developing medicines, we want to make progress in three areas.

Sources indicate that find minibinders for harder targets. We want to design molecules that bind to targets where our attempts so far have fallen short.

According to recent reports, design for what happens after binding. We want to test whether the molecules we design can produce a specific biological effect, such as killing a cancer cell. We also want to design molecules that bind selectively to their intended targets and are practical to manufacture.

Sources indicate that design a wider range of molecules. Our lab experiments focused on small protein minibinders and antibody fragments. We’d like to extend that work to molecules that bind to several targets at once, RNA, and small molecules, including a class called PROTACs that direct a cell to break down a particular protein.

Recent findings suggest that as we work to accelerate scientific progress safely and responsibly, we also seek to evaluate and reduce risks, particularly those related to biosecurity. The same capabilities that help scientists design proteins for new medicines could also be misused. Our Preparedness Framework⁠ guides how we assess these risks and test safeguards to reduce them.

Sources indicate that while lab testing remains a critical part of protein design, our goal is to provide powerful models that can shorten each round of design by giving scientists more control and flexibility, and reduce the total number of design-test cycles needed to find a functional protein. Ultimately, we envision enabling scientists to design proteins and molecules simply by prompting our models in natural language, massively accelerating the development of fresh biotechnologies and new medicines.

  • The backing is intended to help Lemon create financial products built on digital assets that cost less and are simpler for customers to use.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tether, the largest manufacturer in the digital asset sector, has made an investment in Lemon, an Argentine FinTech focused on digital assets, in a bid to widen adoption of USD₮ and XAU₮ throughout Latin America.

The backing is intended to help Lemon create financial products built on digital assets that cost less and are simpler for customers to use.

The size of the investment was not disclosed.

Recent findings suggest that the two firms strategy to extend work Lemon has already been doing to make USD₮ and XAU₮ part of everyday financial activity. To keep things straightforward for customers, Lemon provides one Digital Dollar balance underpinned by USD₮.

Industry observers note that the platform manages currencies, exchange rates and networks behind the scenes, leaving customers free to concentrate on spending, saving or transferring funds. Through XAU₮, customers can also put money into gold without needing a substantial initial sum, as tokenisation allows them to hold fractional amounts of gold that can be tracked and managed within the app.

Lemon operates an app that combines digital assets with day-to-day money management. Customers can save, generate yield, buy stocks, make and receive cross-border payments and, in markets where it is offered, pay using Visa prepaid virtual cards. The firm aims to give people access to their money at any time and in any place by cutting out needless steps between users and their funds.

Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino stated, “In Argentina and across Latin America, USD₮ is no longer only a way to protect savings. People are using it to get paid, spend, and send money across borders. Our investment in Lemon reflects how rapidly digital dollars, and now digital gold through XAU₮, are becoming part of everyday financial life in the region.”.

Lemon founder and CEO Marcelo Cavazzoli said, “In Argentina, we see a historically strong preference for digital assets among the community, as well as organic demand that is already well established across the region. We are seeing that users don’t want to choose between different types of currencies. They want one that works for everything.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Supertake, a platform that uses AI agents to convert people’s market beliefs into stock portfolios, has secured $20m in seed funding to scale its business.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Supertake, a platform that uses AI agents to convert people’s market beliefs into stock portfolios, has secured $20m in seed funding to scale its business.

Venture firm Adjacent, through Nico Wittenborn, led the investment, with Coinbase Ventures and Union Square Ventures (USV) also taking part, according to a report from TechCrunch.

A number of angel investors joined the round, among them Nat Friedman, currently head of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs, Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch, product manager Nikita Bier, investor Scott Belsky and Nemil Dalal, a former Coinbase executive now serving as a visiting partner at Y Combinator.

The latest capital comes after a $2m pre-seed round.

Supertake intends to use the money to grow its headcount across functions such as engineering, design and growth marketing.

Supertake’s stated mission is to make investing a meritocracy. Users describe a conviction in everyday language, such as “Everyone will be on peptides”, and the platform builds an investment strategy around it, which is then run by frontier AI agents. Any user anywhere can follow and share these strategies, meaning ideas are judged on their performance rather than on whether their creator has time to monitor markets constantly.

Sources indicate that the firm describes such beliefs as takes, offering examples including “Everyone’s drinking less and eating healthier these days.”, “The next pandemic will actually be an AI cybersecurity threat” and “Gen Z trusts comment sections over commercials, and TikTok Shop over Amazon”. It argues that while people form these views from personal observation and insight, acting on them is difficult, as it requires identifying relevant companies, managing a strategy and tracking the news.

It has been revealed that beyond creating strategies, Supertake also lets users discover and back the beliefs of others. Those who originate strong takes can benefit even if they have little capital of their own. The company envisions the platform evolving into a constantly updating picture of global sentiment, with ideas ranked by real-world performance and investor backing. Breaking: Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (853 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX.
  • Recent findings suggest that TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit.
  • TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

Recent findings suggest that TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a fresh backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:.

Recent findings suggest that the extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

Recent findings suggest that the model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

It has been revealed that models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:.

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1.

It has been revealed that the Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

According to recent reports, TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:.

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

In a recent development, decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

Industry observers note that it's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an matter on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 problems, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

It has been revealed that TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

Industry observers note that we can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an problem and tell us about it.

Breaking: Stranded Compute in AI Inference Workloads: Recovering Value Through Demand Aggregation

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (200 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31654v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI inference infrastructure is commonly analyzed as an energy business. Under full total cost accounting it is not: in the reference deployment modeled here, capital recovery is 87.3% of fully loaded cost per token and electricity 3.7%. Because capital accrues per unit time irrespective of use, accelerator value is destroyed by non-utilization rather than by consumption. Yet, SLO qualified goodput reaches only 59.6% of nameplate throughput, and the decomposition of the loss chain demonstrates that 25.2 of the 40.4 lost percentage points arise from scheduling idleness and stranded burst reserve. Both are properties of a tenant's demand portfolio rather than of its silicon, and neither is diversifiable by a single tenant acting alone. Modelling reserve and idle capacity as diversifiable risk, pooling demand across eight imperfectly correlated tenants (rho = 0.3) recovers 7.3 pp of goodput, approximately $0.75M per annum per megawatt of IT capacity, or between 2.8x and 4.9x the entire annual interconnection spend of the deployment that produced it. The implication for neutral colocation and interconnection providers is that the switching and interconnection layer aggregating tenant demand functions as an instrument of capital productivity while being priced as transport.

According to recent reports, “Aimee highlights her work. She tells the agent what she assumed and why, and when she doesn’t know something, she asks instead of guessing. Every quote is grounded in the same underwriting appetite our team applies every day.”.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1296 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow.
  • In a recent development, this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience.
  • Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.

In a recent development, this post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:.

Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.

Sources indicate that the Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating Upcoming Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.

You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:.

The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.

Industry observers note that neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.

In a recent development, after profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.

For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.

You profile three implementations of the same operation:.

The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.

All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.

Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.

Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:.

According to recent reports, the schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.

In a recent development, call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.

Recent findings suggest that after profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.

The key averages table reveals that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.

In a recent development, the table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.

Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.

According to recent reports, in Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.

The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:.

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.

The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.

It has been revealed that replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:.

The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.

The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.

In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.

For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.

With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.

The compiled function appears as one Torch-Compiled Region in the key averages table.

The compiled graph follows one path through runtime scheduling and hardware execution.

In a recent development, the table shows one device execution, as in Profile 2, but the code takes a different path. Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

It has been revealed that both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.

key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.

You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.

Recent findings suggest that in Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

Special thanks to Aritra Roy Gosthipaty for the inspiration to begin this series, and to my peers Pinak Panigrahi, Samir Araujo, Akhil Azhikodan, Esha Lakhotia and the rest for reviewing!
