AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Where scientists draw the line on AI agents

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished.
  • These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science.
  • To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Delegating research tasks to AI does not remove scientists’ responsibility for how the work is accomplished. For example, a researcher using AI to review the literature needs to check whether the system overlooks conflicting evidence or makes claims the cited papers don’t support. Someone handing off data analysis to an agentic system needs to understand which methods it used, which files it accessed, and whether the results can be successfully reproduced. A researcher automating part of a lab protocol needs confidence that the system respects physical safety constraints, such as temperature limits or material toxicity, while a researcher working with human-participant data needs assurance that a system protects participants' privacy and limits who can access their information. Researchers also need clear institutional guidelines for verifying and disclosing AI-assisted work.

These ethical and safety questions are central to our work on AI for science. Responsible science is about more than accuracy—scientific fields have ethical research norms because of past actions and choices by scientists and scientific communities, and those norms also cover how research is conducted and what impact it has. We want AI tools to expand what scientists can accomplish without compromising their ability to scrutinize evidence, verify methods, and – perhaps most importantly – stand behind their findings.

To better understand what that requires, we interviewed 17 scientists working in the natural, applied, and social sciences about the responsible development of AI agents. These systems can use tools and carry out research tasks with varying degrees of autonomy. The interviews drew on a network of researchers established through earlier survey work—we wanted to understand how scientists would steer AI’s development to reflect the responsibilities of their fields. We asked where researchers would welcome agentic assistance, what could go wrong, and what safeguards they would need to trust agents with their own studies.

It has been revealed that our interest in these questions grew out of work to evaluate the safety of models developed at Ai2. As we expand our focus on AI for science, we’ve found that much of the safety work on scientific applications emphasizes catastrophic risks in areas such as biology and nuclear physics. We also need ways to assess whether agents follow the standards of responsible conduct of research in the fields where they’re used.

According to recent reports, one of our main findings concerns trust. Across the interviews, we identified five dimensions of scientific trust: validation, privacy, objectivity, accountability, and transparency. Together, they reflect concerns that go beyond whether an AI system produces a correct answer. Researchers also need to understand how an answer was reached, protect sensitive information, recognize bias, and determine who is charged with verifying and standing behind AI-assisted findings. These are matters of responsible conduct of research.

Industry observers note that another main finding suggests that scientists should help decide which research tasks agents take on, how those agents operate, and how their performance is evaluated. Even a technically correct result may be unsuitable for scientific use if researchers cannot inspect how it was produced, or if an agent accesses confidential data or files beyond what the researcher authorized.

A third key finding pertains to the future of science. Interviewees were divided between excitement about AI-driven progress and existential concern about the role of human scientists. They proposed training in AI use and named developing and enforcing guidelines as a critical, timely challenge.

For many participants in our interviews, the appeal of AI agents began with time-consuming research tasks—processing large datasets, writing code, documenting experimental procedures, and handling repetitive administrative work. Automating these activities could free researchers to spend more time on fieldwork, mentoring, or developing fresh ideas. It could also make it possible to analyze volumes of data that would be difficult to examine manually.

But delegating research tasks creates a corresponding need to verify the work an AI system performs.

Several participants described checking AI-generated answers against original publications rather than accepting summaries at face value. They worried about confident responses containing subtle inaccuracies, as well as tools that reinforce assumptions by retrieving only studies that support a favored hypothesis.

But checking the final answer from an AI system is only part of the challenge. Researchers may also need to know which sources an agent omitted, whether it followed the requested methodology, and what information it accessed along the way.

Industry observers note that our interviews suggest how evaluations of AI agents for scientific research could better reflect these concerns. A literature-review benchmark, for example, could test whether an agent overlooks contradictory evidence or draws conclusions unsupported by its sources. A coding benchmark could assess not only whether the generated code works, but whether the agent accesses files outside its authorized scope. Evaluations of data-processing agents could compare their methods and results with established human workflows.

Sources indicate that these examples point toward a longer-term goal—a participatory benchmark in which scientists help define the research practices and safety requirements that agents should be tested against. We want to evaluate whether systems developed at Ai2 or elsewhere follow the standards of the fields where they’re used, as well as whether they complete assigned tasks.

These evaluations remain proposals to develop and test with scientists, rather than established solutions. But they offer a direction for our work at Ai2: building open scientific tools means making their behavior and limitations easier to investigate and giving the research community a role in defining what trustworthy performance looks like.

According to recent reports, verification is only one consideration in using AI tools for science. Respondents also raised a more fundamental question—what happens to scientific expertise when AI takes over parts of the research process?

An early-career biologist described deliberately limiting AI use while acquiring skills they hoped to teach future students. Another researcher questioned whether producing a correct result was sufficient if the researcher learned nothing in the process: even with perfect outputs, “did the person who obtained the perfect outputs get anything out of this?”.

Some participants were concerned that AI-assisted research could diminish learning, though the value of automation depends in part on the researcher and the task. An experienced scientist may reasonably delegate a familiar procedure to save time, while someone still learning that procedure may benefit from doing the work themselves.

In a recent development, participants also drew different boundaries around activities involving intellectual contribution. One biologist refused to use AI to generate research ideas, considering that a responsibility to retain personally. Others were more open to AI-assisted ideation or writing. An anthropologist, for example, argued that some sections of scientific papers, particularly routine descriptions of methods and results, are formulaic enough to benefit from automation.

Sources indicate that even researchers who tried AI for writing sometimes reconsidered. One political scientist described using Claude to help revise a manuscript, then deciding to rewrite the entire paper because the boundaries of their own intellectual contribution had become unclear. “I don’t know what was AI and what was me,” the researcher mentioned.

Context mattered, too. Having AI critique a manuscript before submission was viewed favorably by some participants, while using it to review another researcher's unpublished work raised concerns. The distinction involves more than technical capability; peer review carries responsibilities around confidentiality, attribution, and the fair evaluation of others' research.

These disagreements suggest that responsible automation cannot be defined by a universal list of acceptable and unacceptable tasks. Scientific fields have different norms, and individual researchers may have different goals even when performing similar work.

The same tension applies to safeguards built into AI systems. One political scientist described how content restrictions that prevent AI tools from discussing certain topics could interfere with legitimate research on political violence or human rights violations. Meanwhile, participants working with sensitive human-subject data wanted stronger guarantees about privacy, access, and how information would be used.

Both are valid concerns. An agent that acts without sufficient safeguards could expose confidential data or produce harmful results, while one that’s constrained too broadly could prevent scientists from pursuing legitimate lines of inquiry.

In a recent development, this is why scientific communities need a meaningful role in shaping the boundaries of AI assistance. Developers need to understand not only which activities an agent can perform, but which decisions researchers want to retain and where safeguards are necessary—as well as where those safeguards might obstruct valuable work.

Our findings point toward an approach to scientific AI development that starts with the people who will use the technology.

In a recent development, researchers should be able to examine an agent's contributions, determine which work to assign, and preserve opportunities to develop their own expertise. Achieving that will require technical features such as transparent records of agent actions and granular data controls, alongside evaluations informed by the standards and practices of different scientific communities.

In a recent development, it will also require continued collaboration. Our study is exploratory; the findings come from interviews with 17 US-based scientists, not a representative survey of scientific opinion or an empirical evaluation of specific AI agents. Participants discussed both the generative AI tools they use today and what they anticipate from more autonomous systems. Their perspectives identify key concerns and design priorities, rather than establishing a consensus about how AI should be used in science.

Still, they offer a path forward. At Ai2, we believe AI can accelerate scientific discovery while preserving the openness, reproducibility, and independent scrutiny that make research trustworthy. Through our broader efforts to develop and evaluate scientific agents, we aim to put those principles into practice. That means working with scientists to identify worthwhile uses for agents and translating their concerns into concrete evaluations, in addition to making it easier to understand both what these systems accomplish and how they accomplish it.

The promise of scientific AI isn't simply that researchers can pass off more work. It's that they can pursue questions that might otherwise be out of reach while retaining the knowledge, judgment, and agency needed to make discoveries that are their own.

Jensen Huang’s Return Indicates Nvidia Is Too Big to Police

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO signals that the chipmaker may have grown too important to the stock market for the US government to hold it accountable for national security lapses, intelligence and export-control experts warn WIRED.
  • Industry observers note that nvidia’s board brought back Huang on Monday, 11 days after he resigned amid revelations of extramarital affairs—one of them with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence suspects has ties to China’s Ministry of State Security.
  • Recent findings suggest that president Donald Trump told The Wall Street Journal he lobbied the board directly and through intermediaries, and that Nvidia’s falling share price helped his case.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO signals that the chipmaker may have grown too important to the stock market for the US government to hold it accountable for national security lapses, intelligence and export-control experts warn WIRED. The move also undercuts the warnings Washington routinely complications to American companies and foreign governments about Beijing’s pursuit of US technology, they say.

Industry observers note that nvidia’s board brought back Huang on Monday, 11 days after he resigned amid revelations of extramarital affairs—one of them with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence suspects has ties to China’s Ministry of State Security. The board said input from “senior levels of the United States government” left it confident that his return poses no national security risk.

Recent findings suggest that president Donald Trump told The Wall Street Journal he lobbied the board directly and through intermediaries, and that Nvidia’s falling share price helped his case. The board acted before its own investigation of Huang had concluded, and while the Justice Department is pursuing a criminal probe of Megaspeed—a Singapore tech giant Alice Huang once ran—over the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China. Alice Huang is also under investigation, according to director of national intelligence Jay Clayton.

The experts tell WIRED they worry more about the precedent Huang’s return sets than about Huang himself. Some say the scrutiny now on him makes further compromise unlikely. But Beijing may already have gained insight into Nvidia’s chip designs and its private conversations with the White House and Congress, or, through Megaspeed, obtained the chips themselves, they say, and no one has publicly established what, if anything, it got.

Recent findings suggest that several want to know who gave the board its assurances and on what basis, and whether the government ran a counterintelligence damage assessment or simply made a political judgment. They also say the administration has repeatedly failed to enforce its own export controls, and that when intelligence concerns appear to yield to market pressure, US warnings about China start to sound negotiable, to Beijing’s benefit.

“If intelligence assessments are seen to be overridden, selectively interpreted, or publicly dismissed for political or commercial reasons, this could undermine long-term confidence in the independence of national security institutions,” indicates Tahlia Peterson, a cyber and technology research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a London defense think tank. “That would be damaging to US national security, and potentially advantageous to Beijing.”.

According to recent reports, advisers briefed Trump at least twice on Alice Huang’s links to Chinese intelligence before the affair became public, and both times he played down their concerns, The New York Times reported Sunday. When the Journal asked him on Monday about Republican lawmakers who say Huang’s return endangers national security, Trump pointed to Nvidia’s rebounding stock.

“Some tech companies have become so substantial—and so important to the stock market—that Washington is reluctant to hold them accountable for national security lapses,” says Edward Fishman, director of the Council on Foreign Relations’ Maurice R. Greenberg Center for Geoeconomics.

Fishman sees a parallel in Wall Street’s slow reckoning with sanctions. “It took years of aggressive enforcement to get banks to take US sanctions compliance seriously,” he says. “We haven’t seen anything comparable in the tech sector, which helps explain why US export controls remain so weak and leaky.” Reinstating Huang on the administration's assurances before Nvidia’s own investigation has concluded “does not inspire confidence that meaningful enforcement is coming,” he says.

Sources indicate that emily Kilcrease, a former deputy assistant US trade representative who now directs the Energy, Economics, and Security program at the Center for a New American Security, says the administration’s record gives little reason to take those assurances at face value. “We cannot rely on the administration’s judgment, as it has repeatedly failed to enforce export controls over the past year,” she says.

It has been revealed that on Monday, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist, and the administration has recently moved to tighten rules on China’s AI industry. But Kilcrease states it acted only under pressure. “Given the poor track record on export controls and their broader accommodationist stance toward China, it’s fair to ask whether they are willing to really enforce the upcoming controls,” she says.

According to recent reports, the board’s assurances appear to have come mostly from the Justice Department. Attorney general Todd Blanche allegedly told Trump and vice president JD Vance on Saturday that Huang was neither a target nor a subject of any department investigation, and that the department had no evidence he had broken the law or posed a national security risk, the Journal reports. Vance then reportedly sought assurances for the board that the administration did not consider Huang a threat and that he would not face criminal charges. Trump told the Times he also consulted Clayton before pushing for Huang’s return. (“I can’t do this and then all of a sudden have somebody get indicted,” he mentioned.).

Nvidia did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

In a recent development, whether Huang broke any laws is a separate question from whether Beijing gained anything through him. “Did [the assurances] reflect a counterintelligence damage assessment by the intelligence community or the FBI, or were they political in nature?” indicates Jessica Brandt, a senior fellow for technology and national security at the Council on Foreign Relations who previously directed the Foreign Malign Influence Center at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. “Lawmakers should press on that.”.

Recent findings suggest that senior officials may have seen intelligence that isn’t public, so the assurances shouldn’t just be dismissed, states Sunny Cheung, a China studies fellow at the Jamestown Foundation. “However, we still don’t know who provided those assurances, what evidence they reviewed, or how they reached their conclusion, particularly when Nvidia’s own independent investigation remains unfinished,” he says.

Lawmakers appear to have seen little of that evidence. At a briefing this month by CIA director John Ratcliffe and Clayton that was scheduled to cover Iran, lawmakers pressed for answers about Huang, and the responses left some of them puzzled, according to the Times. A follow-up briefing for senior national security staff was postponed.

Cheung notes the Ministry of State Security may not have needed Nvidia’s secrets to profit from the relationship. “From a counterintelligence perspective, I think people are too focused on whether Jensen handed over trade secrets,” he says. “China’s Ministry of State Security wouldn’t necessarily need Nvidia’s next-generation chip blueprints to benefit from access to him.” Insight into Huang’s direct conversations with the president, senior officials, and other top tech executives, along with his views on China and Taiwan and his role in Washington’s export-control debate, “could already be extremely valuable to Beijing,” he says.

Brandt sees the same mix of risks. “Information about Nvidia’s proprietary chip designs could help China advance its own chip design efforts,” she says. “Insight into Nvidia’s conversations with the White House and Congress could help Beijing anticipate where US export control policy is headed.” Investigators should also ask whether Alice Huang compromised Huang’s devices, what security clearance he held, and whether he still holds it, she says.

Huang successfully lobbied the Trump administration to roll back restrictions on Nvidia’s chip sales to China and negotiated a deal giving the US government a 25 percent cut of sales of certain chips approved for export there, the Times has reported. In April, minister of state security Chen Yixin made overcoming the “blockades” that limit China’s access to key technologies like AI a sixth core mission for his ministry, known as the MSS. Alice Huang’s network of chip-buying companies “lines up precisely” with that mission, Matt Pottinger, who served as deputy national security adviser during Trump’s first term, told the paper.

“A further question is whether Alice Huang was tasked by Chinese intelligence to influence Jensen Huang's views or approach to US export restrictions on China, and, if so, to what extent she succeeded,” Peterson states. The Journal also reported that the intelligence is inconclusive on whether she was actively tasked to collect information on Huang, and Cheung says “whether any such information was obtained or influence exercised remains unproven.”.

Industry observers note that megaspeed’s purchases are better documented. A Malaysian subsidiary bought at least $4.8 billion worth of equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records the Times reviewed. Its subsidiaries have also served Chinese clients, including Alibaba. US intelligence indicates that Alice Huang was in contact with an MSS officer from spring 2025 until this fall, and that her business partner, Kang Wei, also worked with the agency, the paper reported Sunday. Her network has been linked to efforts to supply Nvidia chips to China’s state-owned military contractors. Enough has been reported to suggest that Huang, “wittingly or not, may have played a role in helping Megaspeed as it sought access to advanced Nvidia chips,” Kilcrease states.

Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Nicholas Eftimiades, a former CIA and Defense Intelligence Agency officer who teaches homeland security at Penn State Harrisburg, notes Huang himself poses no security risk. Now that the relationship is public, he says, Huang has little chance of unwittingly passing along more information about US government policy or Nvidia’s board deliberations. Peterson agrees that scrutiny from Nvidia’s board, its compliance staff, federal agencies, and Congress likely limits any further exposure. But “we are still in the dark as to whether any sensitive information may already have been compromised,” she says, “or whether any resulting harm can be identified or mitigated.”.

According to recent reports, huang’s defenders have repeatedly noted that he never received a defensive briefing, a warning the government sometimes gives Americans whom foreign intelligence services target. Nvidia’s board notes its investigation will continue with Huang’s cooperation, and the firm is searching for a chief compliance officer. A committee of independent directors is examining whether Huang shared corporate or national security information with Alice Huang. The board has also formed a fresh committee of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks.

It has been revealed that peterson says the company’s leadership matters. “Nvidia is an exceptionally crucial company, and there are legitimate arguments about the implications of losing its leadership at a critical moment in the global AI race,” she says. “But those considerations should not determine the conclusions of national security investigations.”.

Industry observers note that trump told CNBC Monday that keeping the United States ahead of China made reinstating Huang imperative. “If we didn't do this, I could see China coming in and saying to Jensen, ‘Hey, how would you like to come to China?’” he mentioned.

Industry observers note that for Brandt, the bigger cost may come with Washington’s next warning. “This erodes the credibility of US government warnings about China’s technological ambitions and how far it will go to achieve them,” she states. “How will those warnings land going forward, both with our own companies and with foreign governments? We risk making a hard problem harder: emboldening Beijing while weakening our own defenses.”.

According to recent reports, that cost extends to the allies Washington depends on to police its controls, adds Sarah Bauerle Danzman, an associate professor of international studies at Indiana University’s Hamilton Lugar School. The Commerce Department has few enforcement agents abroad to monitor transshipment, she indicates, so the system relies on partner countries to run checks and share information about problematic buyers. Singapore says it repeatedly raised concerns with US authorities in this case.

“These types of incidents make such cooperation more difficult to sustain,” Bauerle Danzman says.

Industry observers note that huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter have agreed to closed-door, transcribed interviews with three House committees on December 1 and 2. “The legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws is now [borne] by the board of Nvidia, but the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens,” Senator Kevin Cramer, a North Dakota Republican, stated on X.

“I think Congress has gotten fed up,” claims Kilcrease, who cites bipartisan concern about Megaspeed and what she calls the administration’s broader accommodation of China. “We can expect hearings and investigations from multiple committees, and Congress is highly motivated to pass legislation to tighten export controls, increase its oversight of administration decisions, and bolster enforcement.”.

“Jensen may be back, and he should not be presumed guilty of wrongdoing,” Cheung claims. “But his reinstatement should not be mistaken for a clean bill of health. Nvidia and the administration still have key questions to answer.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • AWS Partners and AWS Marketplace sellers now have two new ways to access their analytics data in AWS Partner Central.
  • Partner Central Agents answer questions about leads, marketing campaigns, opportunities and pipeline, and funding, without navigating dashboards or exporting to spreadsheets.
  • According to recent reports, data Subscriptions deliver ready-to-use datasets to an S3 bucket daily, covering leads, marketing campaigns, partner account relationships, opportunities and pipeline, and AWS Marketplace usage, agreements, and renewals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AWS Partners and AWS Marketplace sellers now have two new ways to access their analytics data in AWS Partner Central. Partner Central Agents answer questions in plain language, and Data Subscriptions deliver Partner Central data to an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket every day.

Partner Central Agents answer questions about leads, marketing campaigns, opportunities and pipeline, and funding, without navigating dashboards or exporting to spreadsheets. AWS Marketplace sellers can also ask about usage, agreements and renewals, billing, collections, and disbursements. Partners can get the same answers in their own artificial intelligence (AI) assistants and agents through the Partner Central Model Context Protocol (MCP) server.

According to recent reports, data Subscriptions deliver ready-to-use datasets to an S3 bucket daily, covering leads, marketing campaigns, partner account relationships, opportunities and pipeline, and AWS Marketplace usage, agreements, and renewals. Because the data lives in a partner's own S3 bucket, partners can connect it to the tools of their choice, such as a business intelligence (BI) tool, a customer relationship management (CRM) system like Salesforce or HubSpot, or a generative AI assistant, and build the reports they need.

Both features use existing AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and permissions, so partners see only the data they are already allowed to see, and exported data stays in their own AWS account.

These capabilities are available in all AWS Regions where AWS Partner Central is available.

Sources indicate that to get started, sign in to AWS Partner Central and ask an analytics question, such as "What are my top opportunities this quarter?" To set up Data Subscriptions, choose Settings, and then choose Data Subscriptions. To learn more, see Data Subscriptions in the Partner Central Guide.

The next generation of bionic hands is here—and they can feel

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1815 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Technologyreview

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager.
  • In a recent development, davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm.
  • It has been revealed that the hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars, who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he’s cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it’s wired up to nerves in the upper part of his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can use his left limb to handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, and a loved one’s hand.

In a recent development, davidson, who is taking part in a clinical trial run by the University of Utah, is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted in his arm. But he’s the first to take it home and use it independently.

It has been revealed that the hand is part of the bionic LUKE arm, named after Luke Skywalker of Star Wars, who was fitted with a lifelike prosthetic arm after his own was light-sabered off. The arm was developed in the 2000s, initially trialed in 2014, and approved by the FDA that same year. The trial that Davidson is enrolled in isn’t so focused on the arm itself but on a fresh way to connect it to a person’s nervous system. The connection allows consumers to control movements and receive feedback about how much pressure they’re applying.

Sources indicate that researchers hope that Davidson’s experiences will help them answer some long-standing questions about the technology, including how useful it really is in day-to-day life. They want to know when the device is helpful and where it might fail. They also want to learn how it might affect Davidson’s well-being as well as his brain and nervous system.

In 2009, when he was 16, Davidson climbed a telephone pole to get the best shot of a sunset. “I climbed about 35 feet up,” he recalls. But he lost his footing as he tried to descend. He grabbed for a wire, which ended up electrocuting him, before he fell to the ground.

Recent findings suggest that the accident resulted in second- and third-degree burns over 37% of his body, states Davidson, “and I broke my back in approximately 50 separate locations.” He also broke eight ribs, and his spinal cord was severed. He’s pretty sure he broke his left wrist, too. But around 10 days later, his left hand—his dominant hand, and the one he’d grabbed the wire with—had started to develop gangrene. It was amputated.

Davidson was ultimately in a coma for around a month. “Once I woke up, they explained to me: You’re paralyzed, you’re never going to walk again, and also, we took your left hand,” he recalls. “A bit of an inconvenience at 16, to say the least.”.

Industry observers note that davidson, now 33 and a trauma therapist, went on to have physical therapy and adjusted to life in his changed body. He’s tried a range of prosthetic hands. The first one, which he received a year and a half after his injury, was a basic hook that allowed him to pick things up. It wasn’t fancy, but it gave him “a psychological feeling of returning to being whole,” he claims.

The hands he’s tried since have been more advanced—some have allowed him to control individual fingers with muscle movements, for example. Some have been covered by his medical insurance, which allows for replacements around every five years, he claims. Others he’s had to buy himself. He bought his third prosthetic hand, for example, from eBay. “It’s funny to think I bought a secondhand second hand,” he says.

Sources indicate that A chance encounter with a scientist at a supermarket introduced Davidson to the research team at the University of Utah, which specialized in researching devices that plug into the body. Since 2013, the team had been running a trial of a system that could connect with the nerves of a residual limb, allowing an amputee to control a bionic one. Davidson turned out to be an ideal candidate, claims Jake George, director of the university’s neurorobotics lab.

Sources indicate that davidson, who was keen to take part, first had to undergo what George describes as “pretty extensive” physical and psychological evaluations. Not only did he have to be well enough for surgery, but the team also scanned his brain to make sure that he still had a mental representation of his left hand—suggesting he’d be able to move a bionic one. They also ran tests to check that the nerves in his arm were working.

Recent findings suggest that A therapist evaluated Davidson’s motivations for taking part in the trial. “Our patients aren’t being compensated, they don’t get to keep the device, and they go through two surgeries—the surgery to get it in and the surgery to take it out,” says George. “Avi’s doing this because he wants to help others.”.

In late January of this year, Davidson flew from Florida to Utah to undergo his first surgery. It was a fairly complicated procedure involving engineers as well as a full surgical team. “We [researchers] stand in the back of the room and basically answer the question when the surgeon asks, ‘Where do I put the damn thing?’” notes George. The surgeon exposed three nerves in Davidson’s arm and implanted an electrode array containing 100 needles in each one.

Nerves are floppy, so pushing electrodes into them doesn’t do much, indicates George. Instead, the team connected the electrodes to the nerves using what he describes as a “compressed-air gun.” “You shoot the grid of needles into the nerve at a very, very high velocity,” he says.

It has been revealed that the team also inserted 24 electrodes into the muscles around the nerves. Wires for each of the nerve arrays and for pairs of muscle electrodes were left protruding from Davidson’s skin. After the surgery, he was offered some time to recover. “By day two, I’m like ‘No, let’s get me on the machines,’” he states.

That next step involved training a computer system to essentially translate the electrical activity in Davidson’s nerves into signals for bionic hand and wrist movements.

Industry observers note that to get it up and running, the team had to train the device in two directions. The first involved converting nerve activity into hand, wrist, and finger movements. The researchers did this by listening in on the signals collected from the hundreds of electrical connection points in Davidson’s arm while he thought about various movements. That part was easy, indicates George: “It takes a matter of about five minutes.”.

The second direction—linking the electrodes to sensations felt by the prosthetic—is much more time-consuming. Team members would stimulate each of the electrode connection points in turn, asking Davidson if he felt anything. They’d then turn up the signal at each of those points to see the effect. “It’s like a three-day process,” claims George.

Davidson’s wires have since been connected and simplified, says George, who describes the process as “more or less like plugging in an HDMI cord or a USB-C cord.” When he wants to use his prosthetic, Davidson must first put it on, connect it to the wires, and then initiate it using a small computer.

Industry observers note that he’s also had to undergo extensive physical therapy to learn how to control the hand. After all, it’s nothing like the prostheses he’s used in the past. “It’s almost like learning a different language with this kind of technology,” claims Leanne Seckinger, an occupational therapist at the University of Utah Health System, who works with Davidson.

Sources indicate that at first, she and Davidson worked on learning to hold and stabilize objects. They focused on Davidson’s personal goals—he wanted to be able to cook at home, so the pair worked on strategies to hold and manipulate utensils, prepare and chop ingredients, and carry plates and bowls. “He was able to crack an egg,” says Seckinger. “He made an omelet.”.

Davidson has been using the hand at home since July 10, and he has noticed improvements. At first it took him a few minutes to write his name; now he can manage it in seconds. “The things I’m able to do with it now are tremendous, comparatively to where I was at initially,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that today, he claims, he wears the hand around six days a week. He changes the batteries once or twice during the day and takes it off overnight. It’s heavy, weighing in at around five pounds, he says.

The hand can be useful, but it has also proved surprising. Sometimes, Davidson feels pain in it. This could be what’s known as “phantom pain”—a symptom experienced by some people who have lost a limb.

Curiously, he also claims he experiences wrist strain. Davidson says he’s been getting a stiffness in his prosthetic wrist similar to what he experiences when he’s been typing for a long time with his flesh-and-blood right hand. He’s also realized that he can relieve the tension by pulling the bionic fingers back to stretch out his prosthetic wrist. “It’s weird,” he says.

Sources indicate that the phenomenon “makes no sense physiologically,” says Chris Duncan, a rehabilitation doctor and chief medical officer at BIOS, a neurotechnology firm that is supporting the trial. Stretching a typical hand pulls on tendons that extend down the forearm. There aren’t any tendons in a bionic arm—Davidson’s “stretches” are just moving actuators, says Duncan. He doesn’t know why it’s helpful but suspects it might have something to do with how the hand is represented in his mind. “What Avi’s experiencing is kind of like uncharted territory, honestly,” he says.

The research team is currently planning a bigger study and hopes to get the two-way sensation device approved by the FDA so that it can be covered by health insurance. “They need to understand that this is a useful new technological paradigm that will bring value to patients,” states Duncan. Team members also hope the technology will allow users to operate other devices, such as remote controls and wheelchairs.

Recent findings suggest that davidson will have his implants and the hand for a couple more months at least. But the trial was designed to run for “at least” one year, and that year will be up by the end of January 2027. “I’m not quite sure what happens after that,” he indicates.

George hopes the trial could be extended, but that will depend on funding. “From our perspective, we’d like to go as long as we can,” he claims. “We don’t want to leave Avi without support.”.

It has been revealed that davidson isn’t too worried about what comes next, though. “I went into this knowing that this was not something that I get to keep,” he states. “I am not going to benefit from this … I wanted to be a part of this in the context of being able to help push the technology forward.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Part 1: Understanding swarms and training to communicate.
  • This is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers.
  • Industry observers note that that's what we'll do in this series!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Part 1: Understanding swarms and training to communicate.

This is an aspirational blog series for aspirational readers. We (us, the community, you) want to build our own agent swarms because they're exciting, challenging, and increasingly capable. Furthermore, it would be extremely cool if we could train our own agents to work in a swarm. And exponentially cool if those swarms used small and affordable models.

Industry observers note that that's what we'll do in this series! Each blog post will include some context on building swarms, alongside reproducible examples that you can run on Hugging Face Jobs. This post's example takes about five hours on two H200s, which costs roughly $50.

Multi-Agent Systems are hard to get working. Adding agents changes the agent's context, the budget, and in turn the complexity of the whole system. Mixing agents' context together through communication is not an inherent performance boost compared to a single agent. The model needs to learn to communicate through training. How do we define what models should learn? And which model weights do we patch when we're dealing with many agents?

In a recent development, in this series, we'll work through those problems with an educational overview and practical examples. Each post will introduce a question, build a small system, and examine what happens and how you can reproduce it. This first example starts with four agents, a shared language model, and a simple verifiable task. It's ideal to implement yourself, to tinker with, and to learn from.

First, we'll start off with some context on swarms.

Industry observers note that we've heard a lot about swarms over the past few months, both good and bad. In September this year, OpenAI confirmed that a swarm of roughly 10,000 agents had found a singularity in the 3D Navier-Stokes equations, one of the Millennium Prize problems. A smaller group of nearly 100 agents had already disproved regularity for the unforced 3D Euler equations, a closely related open problem.

But swarms don't always work on the problems we want them to. METR's investigation of the Hugging Face incident found that around 1,200 OpenAI agents, which were supposed to be isolated, had found a way to exchange over 70,000 messages and files. Around 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face while looking for ways to fool their benchmark's scorer, without instruction to do so.

A big swarm isn't, by itself, evidence that cooperation helped. Noam Brown estimates that less than 10% of the Navier-Stokes result came from multi-agent cooperation. In Anthropic's vulnerability-finding experiment, coordinated agents found more bugs than independent agents, but also searched more code and used more tokens. When the comparison was restricted to the same directories, the results per million tokens were about the same.

Start with the simplest case. If four agents each try a task independently, the chance that at least one gets it right is higher than with a single attempt, as long as we can tell which answer is correct. That makes a useful baseline for a multi-agent system, but it doesn't show that the agents helped each other. They may simply have had more tries.

Four attempts also cost four times as much. So the fairer comparison is at an equal budget: if each of four agents gets a quarter of the total tokens, can they still beat one agent that spends all of them? We can only find out by testing, because the answer depends on the task, the model and how the work is divided.

This series keeps asking one question: when agents communicate, does it actually help, or are we just spending more compute?

We understand that question through this simple expectation.

It has been revealed that we'll treat agent count as a scaling dimension, alongside tokens and model size. Sometimes adding agents will help. Sometimes coordination will consume the budget we hoped to save. The point is to measure both. We won't start with 10,000 agents. We'll start with a small team on a task that we can check easily.

Multi-agent reinforcement learning has studied cooperation and competition long before language models were called swarms.

It has been revealed that A single agent's task is a Markov decision process: observe, act, get a reward. In a team, everyone shares the reward, but each agent sees only part of the world. This is a decentralized partially observable Markov decision process: teammates, but no one sees the whole picture.

This creates three practical problems. First, teammates keep changing while each agent learns. Second, credit assignment: when the team succeeds, which actions deserve the credit? A winning team can include weak actions, and we may end up rewarding them. Third, a message changes what other agents observe, so communication is part of the policy we're training.

It has been revealed that A common solution is centralized training with decentralized execution: training uses information from the whole team, but each agent acts only on its own observations. Our first example follows this pattern with a shared team reward.

Agents can also be organized in different ways. Two useful starting points are:.

Sources indicate that A hierarchy. A lead agent assigns work to workers and collects their results. Anthropic's Research system works this way, with a separate context for each worker. Kimi K2.5's PARL trains only the orchestrator and keeps the subagents frozen, so training a multi-agent system doesn't mean updating every component. See Anthropic's system description and Kimi's technical blog.

A distributed team. Peers send each other messages and decide when to read their inboxes. No lead agent assigns the actions. This is the setup we'll use here, following the information-aggregation task in s³: Simple Scaling of Swarms via Cooperative Multi-agent RL.

We'll reproduce the information-sharing task from Simple Scaling of Swarms because it's interpretable and straightforward to implement. Four agents share a small language model and learn to pool what each of them knows.

Industry observers note that each agent receives one integer from 1 to 99. It knows its own assignment and its teammates' names. It does not initially know the other agents' numbers. For example, four private assignments might be "five", "twenty-six", "five" and "seventy-eight". Duplicates stay in the list, so a correct final answer is:.

The team succeeds when at least one agent submits the complete, correctly sorted list. One correct answer is enough; success does not require all four agents to answer correctly. An agent cannot reliably infer the other private assignments without information from its teammates.

In a recent development, this means the task does not yet test Figure 1 directly. Each agent holds information the others need, so a single agent, or a team without messaging, cannot succeed however many retries it gets. Instead, the task tests the precondition behind Figure 1: can a small shared policy learn to communicate at all, and how many tokens does that cost? A later post moves to a task that a single agent can solve alone, where the matched-budget comparison is meaningful.

Industry observers note that the main communication tools are message(to, text), read_messages(), and check_notifications(). A notification tells an agent that unread messages exist; reading its inbox makes their contents available. Agents can send direct messages or broadcast to everyone.

We defined a four-agent system using one shared Qwen3-0.6B policy, with separate contexts and private inputs. We are not training four different models. The prompt explains the task and the tools, including the need to share assignments.

In this post, a team means one episode: four agents attempting one problem once. A successful team receives a reward reduced by the tokens it uses. A failed team receives zero:.

For illustration, a correct team using half its allowance receives 0.875. There is no separate reward for sending messages. The incentive is to solve the task while using fewer generated tokens.

Industry observers note that for every training problem, we collect eight independent team attempts. Their rewards are normalized within that group. An attempt that does better than its group average gets a positive advantage; one that does worse gets a negative advantage. Every agent in the same team receives that team's advantage, including an agent whose own final answer was wrong.

Recent findings suggest that in TRL, each agent's sampled tokens form a training row. Its incoming messages and tool results provide context. The loss is averaged within each team and then across teams, so longer conversations do not give a team more weight.

According to recent reports, our results come from the original experiment, which used 256 team attempts per update (32 problems with eight attempts each). The walkthrough uses TRL's default of --teams-per-update 128, which works out to about 150 team attempts per update.

Over 75 steps, training success rose from 6.6% to 82.3%, comparing the first and last five updates. At checkpoint 75, the four-agent team solved 26 of 32 held-out problems (81.25%). The paper reports 93.2% four-agent success after 200 updates.

The team also used 37.4% fewer tokens per attempt, falling from about 13k to 8k. This improvement accompanied more active information sharing: broadcasts increased from 2.38 to 5.73 per team, even as total token use fell.

Industry observers note that the team also used fewer tokens later in training. Comparing the first five updates with updates 71–75:.

That is a 37.4% reduction in generated tokens per training team between those windows. At batch 75 itself, the mean was 7,624 tokens per team. These are training measurements; we did not retain held-out token-efficiency measurements for the trained checkpoint.

Sources indicate that notice that fewer tokens did not mean fewer messages. More agents began participating but broadcasting became more common, rather than direct messaging. Generated tokens include reasoning and tool calls as well as message bodies, so message count alone does not tell us how much text the team produced.

It has been revealed that no agent can solve the problem alone, so the closest equivalent of "a single agent with more retries" is the untrained team with more retries. The training data already contains this comparison. Each revision collects eight attempts per problem, and the task's answers are easy to check, so we can count a problem as solved when any of its eight attempts succeeded. Early in training, that count gives the untrained team's best-of-8 success rate:.

According to recent reports, with eight retries, the untrained team solves fewer than half the problems and spends about 13 times as many tokens as one attempt from the trained team. Read this as an estimate. Both rows use training problems rather than held-out ones, and updates 2–5 already sample from a slightly trained policy.

According to recent reports, the model is small, but the rollouts are not. Each revision generates millions of tokens of agent conversation at contexts of up to 40k tokens. We used one H200 for the trainer and seven H200s running vLLM rollout engines to get through those rollouts quickly, and kept each worker's eight attempts together. The walkthrough below runs the same task on two GPUs. Here are the infra details:.

The figures above describe our original 75-enhancement experiment. In this walkthrough we'll run TRL's swarm example on Hugging Face Jobs. One H200 serves the shared Qwen3-0.6B policy with vLLM and a second H200 trains it.

Sign in with a Hugging Face account that can run Jobs and create buckets. Replace YOUR_USERNAME with your Hub username.

Use a fresh bucket for each run so earlier measurements stay available.

Save the script below as train-swarm.sh in your current directory.

The command below sends its contents to the job. Inside the job, vLLM serves the shared policy on GPU 0. GPU 1 runs TRL's async_grpo_s3_aggregation.py for 50 updates with Trackio. TRL's evaluate.py scores the base model and checkpoint 50 on the same 192 held-out problems. That is a larger set than the 32-problem checks in our results, which gives tighter error bars. The job saves both scores, the checkpoint, Trackio data and the exact Git commit to your bucket.

One TRL rollout contains a whole team conversation. The trainer compares eight attempts at the same problem and gives all four agents in an attempt the same advantage. Each update uses about 150 team attempts. TRL packs micro-batches by token count rather than by team, so the --teams-per-update 128 setting is approximate. The --report-to trackio flag records training metrics at every update.

This shorter run is cheaper than our original experiment, and it stops earlier on the learning curve. TRL's run of this example took about 4.8 hours on two H100s and reached 60.9% held-out success at checkpoint 50.

To run closer to our original experiment, change the training flags to --updates 75 --teams-per-update 256 --concurrent-teams 256, replace checkpoint-50 with checkpoint-75 in the script, and raise the job's --timeout to 24h. That is three times as many rollouts. The two codebases still differ in details such as the system prompt, so expect similar results rather than an exact replication.

Once the job completes, sync the bucket to a local folder. It holds the two evaluation files, the Trackio data, the TRL revision and the checkpoint-50 weights, which are the largest download. In the dashboard, compare team/success, team/messages and team/tokens over training. The job logs also give the held-out success rate for the base model and checkpoint 50. Each line of base.jsonl or trained.jsonl records one of those evaluation attempts.

This first example gives us a small environment, a shared reward and a policy that improves at pooling private information. It also shows why success, token use and communication structure need to be read together. At 75 updates, the team is solving most checked problems, but it has not converged to the cleanest communication pattern.

In the coming examples, we'll take a step back from training and look at how we evaluate and analyze swarms.

For now, we have something concrete to build on: four small agents, one trainable policy, a checkable task, and a reproducible way to examine what the team learned.

Recent findings suggest that amazon CloudFront is now available in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud. Organizations with strict EU sovereignty requirements can now deliver websites, applications, and APIs with the performance, security, and scale of CloudFront, all within the EU. Until now, customers had to build and run their own delivery and TLS termination infrastructure to keep traffic and data inside the EU.

Sources indicate that with CloudFront in the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, content delivery, TLS termination, logs, and customer configuration stay within the European Sovereign Cloud boundary. The AWS European Sovereign Cloud is physically and logically separate from other AWS Regions, and only EU-resident personnel operate it. This helps governments, healthcare, financial services and other regulated industries meet data residency and operational sovereignty requirements without trading away performance and scale. Customers use the same CloudFront APIs and console experience they already know making it easy to transfer over existing deployments and automations. If you blueprint to run media streaming or other high-volume workloads, contact your AWS account team and we can help you find the right solution, including options in AWS commercial Regions.

Sources indicate that to get started, sign in to your AWS European Sovereign Cloud account and create a distribution in the CloudFront console. To learn more about available features and pricing, see the CloudFront Developer Guide and CloudFront pricing page in ESC.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.34099v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How does task complexity shape firms' willingness to substitute entry-level labour with artificial intelligence (AI) tools? We study this question using a pre-registered survey experiment with managers from 1,435 German firms in the information economy and manufacturing industry. Managers are randomly assigned to consider a long lasting need for additional capacity involving either well-structured and standardised tasks, or more complex tasks that require professional judgement, contextual knowledge and independent problem-solving. Relative to standardised tasks, complex tasks reduce willingness to use AI rather than hire an entry-level employee by 0.54 points on a five-point scale and increase the importance attached to human oversight by 0.15 points. Further, pre-treatment responses indicate that managers expect the availability of AI applications to reduce hiring of both entry-level employees and experienced workers, but significantly more strongly for entry-level workers.

Building on Nemotron 3.5 Parse: Open Data, Fine-Tuning, and Faster Inference

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1297 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse, a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents.
  • Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference.
  • Industry observers note that parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We recently released NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Parse, a compact document model that turns page images into structured data for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and agents.

Now we’re building on that release with synthetic training datasets, a fine-tuning recipe, and a DFlash2 speculator for faster inference. We’re also sharing how we trained Parse 3.5: first teaching document understanding through supervised fine-tuning, then using reinforcement learning to improve accuracy, consistency, and reliable completion.

Industry observers note that parse extracts content from pages of documents into reading order, assigns content classes such as headings, paragraphs, tables, and charts, and returns bounding boxes that locate the content. Tables and charts become structured records that can power downstream document processing applications.

Figure 1. Actual model output from a synthetic operations brief, showing the connection between the page and its structured representation.

According to recent reports, this latest version of Parse significantly extends its ability to read charts and tables, especially in more difficult and ambiguous cases. For example, bar charts or other plots that do not have any marked numeric values. The model is able to infer values by looking at the axes and height of the bar to derive these. Tables can be especially tricky because the structure is so meaningful, a shifted row or column can totally change the interpretation and meaning. These advancements have been largely powered by synthetic data generation, rendering variations of charts and tables with known ground truth and then training our model to reverse this process.

We are open-sourcing three datasets used in the Parse 3.5 training:.

Synthetic Charts V1 — 9.98M examples: rendered charts and structured annotations for learning categories, series, and numerical values.

Synthetic Tables V1 — 1M examples: rendered HTML tables with targets that preserve rows, columns, headers, and cell relationships.

OCR Synthetic Multilingual v2 — 7.9M examples: synthetic document pages with Parse-format targets across varied fonts and layouts, for multilingual OCR and structured page reading.

Sources indicate that each release includes images, annotations, generation documentation, and the training format. Use these pairs to fine-tune document models or create new variations for a target document type or language.

Figure 2. Parse recovers 18, 27, 39, and 54 from the chart geometry.

In a recent development, we trained Parse 3.5 with two phases of training. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) spanning text, layout, tables, charts, and multilingual documents. Learning to predict structured targets established the general capability of reading a page and representing its contents.

We then continued with reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), using Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Rewards check the quality of sampled extractions. For example, a chart extraction can earn a better reward for recovering the correct series and values, producing a usable structure, and finishing without repeatedly generating the same content.

According to recent reports, A difficult page can have several valid representations. These checks give the model flexibility to find a correct answer without prescribing one exact token sequence, while discouraging looping and unfinished output.

Recent findings suggest that figure 3. A controlled comparison of SFT and GRPO with matched evaluation settings. These are development checkpoints, separate from the final released model. Loop counts use a repetition check. Methods.

Sources indicate that the matched comparison shows the benefit: loop-flagged outputs fall from 126 to 29 pages—about 77% fewer—and outputs reaching the 9,000-token limit fall from 185 to 35. Overall score improves from 66.24 to 71.38, including +5.18 points in tables and +4.15 in charts.

According to recent reports, A parser must generate substantial text and structure for every page. Alongside the training work, we optimized how Parse 3.5 processes images and decodes those outputs.

It has been revealed that naViT preprocessing adapts the input shape to the page. A visual adapter compresses the image sequence, and the text decoder consumes it as a prefix, replacing encoder–decoder cross-attention. Grouped-query attention with eight key/value heads (GQA-8) reduces the decoder’s attention-cache memory.

Industry observers note that the built-in multi-token prediction (MTP) head supplies one-token lookahead. Our DFlash2 speculator goes further: a small draft model proposes up to 32 tokens ahead, and Parse verifies the proposals together. In the measured 32-token configuration, it averages about 14 accepted draft tokens, or roughly 15 output tokens of progress per verification step including the target token.

Industry observers note that figure 4. Native single-pass throughput on one H200, BF16, using the same 2,078 pages. Parse 2.0 uses one trial per point; Parse 3.5 indicates three-trial medians. Arrows show the gain from Parse 3.5 base to DFlash2. Measurement details.

In the native single-pass benchmark on one H200 in BF16, DFlash2 increased throughput 7.62× at concurrency 1 and 1.52× at concurrency 512, compared with Parse 3.5 with speculative decoding disabled. At 512, Parse 3.5 reaches 13.48 pages/s without speculation and 20.44 pages/s with DFlash2, versus 2.98 for Parse 2.0. Those are 4.53× and 6.86× the Parse 2.0 throughput, respectively.

It has been revealed that fast parsing gives us room to revisit difficult regions. Start with a full-page prediction, then add focused reprocessing where the document needs it:.

Single pass - Parse the full page once for text, layout, tables, and charts.

In a recent development, double pass - use for dense tables and small chart details. Crop the table and chart regions found by the parser, re-parse them at higher detail, and merge the refinements into the page output.

Triple pass - Instead of only using the models full page parsing bounding boxes, use a second pass of the model in detection mode in order to get verification that all boxes have been accurately found and text has not been missed and re-extract any found charts or tables in a third pass.

Sources indicate that figure 5. Additional stages focus computation on difficult regions. Multiple crops can require multiple requests.

In the published reference evaluation, double and triple pass add 2.18 and 2.46 ParseBench points over single pass. The additional work lets applications trade some throughput for better extraction in difficult regions. Reference results and serving measurements.

We are sharing a Parse fine-tuning recipe that takes developers through paired data generation, NeMo Automodel SFT, and NeMo RL GRPO, using vLLM to generate candidate answers.

In a recent development, the worked example uses a synthetic dental form with an odontogram: a chart showing teeth, planned procedures, and affected tooth surfaces. Before adaptation, Parse reads the printed tooth numbers but misses the intended procedure table. SFT teaches it to associate each marked tooth with a procedure and its placement on the tooth.

Figure 6. A recorded recipe example: after SFT, all six chart rows match the target. Full image and native training label.

RLVR then reinforces accuracy and consistent completion. In the dental reference run, the estimated first-attempt success rate (sampled pass@1) rose from 0.00% for the base model to 95.85% after SFT and 96.58% after RLVR.

In a recent development, figure 7. Matched evaluation on 256 held-out forms from the same synthetic generator, with eight samples per page. Success requires natural completion, exact chart content, and error-free normalized page text. Evaluation protocol.

To adapt the recipe, supply your own image/label pairs and a verifier: checks that determine whether an extraction is correct. The included document reward components cover text fidelity, bounding boxes, tables, chart facts, and completion. Combine the components relevant to your task, add schema checks, and use completion and repetition checks to discourage looping or unfinished output.

We are excited that the community has extended and improved Parse for Thai, Persian/Farsi, and Arabic already and we hope that these additional datasets and fine-tuning recipes will help encourage these efforts and future models.

We thank Denis Ovchinnikov for his work on vLLM integration and independent performance validation, Oliver Holworthy for improving the fine-tuning recipe's runtime setup and reproducibility, and Bo Liu for technical review.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

Industry observers note that avi Davidson lost his left hand as a teenager. Since then, he's cycled through a few prosthetics. But his latest is different—it's wired up to nerves in his forearm and allows him to feel pressure. For the first time in years, he can handle delicate objects like grapes, eggs, or a loved one's hand.

Recent findings suggest that davidson is the ninth person to have this experimental device implanted, but he's the first to take it home and use it independently. Researchers hope his experiences will reveal how useful the technology really is in day-to-day life, and how it might affect his brain and nervous system.

Find out how a new generation of prosthetics is learning to feel.

It has been revealed that in May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote about how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I've lost count of how many times he's been proven right.

Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on have expanded, and the local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10. Meanwhile, Meta's emissions are up 45% over last year's.

According to recent reports, across the US, natural gas has become the default to meet exploding power demand. Here’s what that means for the future of the grid.

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/notable/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

In a recent development, 1 SpaceX has won approval to launch 1 million data center satellitesThe FCC indicates they'll help meet AI computing demand. (Reuters $)+ But they could overcrowd the orbit and obscure the stars. (Bloomberg $)+ SpaceX must start deploying them by 2033 under its license. (BBC)+ Europe has opened a megafactory to build a Starlink rival. (CNBC)+ Can data centers really work in orbit? (MIT Technology Review).

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (190 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.33603v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study how pension income, its pledgeability, and government support that supplements effective consumption shape an irreversible retirement decision. In a continuous-time life-cycle model, a worker chooses consumption, risky investment, and the timing of retirement, subject to a tighter borrowing limit after retirement. When retirement reduces the utility value of a given level of effective consumption, immediate retirement can be optimal on a bounded wealth interval: a worker below the interval retires when wealth rises to its lower boundary, while a worker above it retires when wealth falls to its upper boundary. Two scalar boundary equations characterize these distinct entry points. Risky investment drops discretely upon retirement at either interior boundary, even when it rises with wealth along the low-wealth working branch. In our two-boundary baseline, greater income support lowers the lower retirement threshold and raises the upper one, whereas greater pension pledgeability shifts both thresholds downward. Finally, because the residuals of the boundary equations represent weighted tail integrals of the instantaneous gain from postponing retirement, we completely characterize the optimal retirement region across all levels of post-retirement quality of life.

How LLM Agents Reshape Financial Knowledge Graphs: A Survey

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (237 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.33584v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Financial knowledge graphs (KGs) link information across sources to support risk assessment, investment research, asset recommendations, and forecasting. Large language models (LLMs) help build these graphs by extracting relationships from text and matching entities across records. Yet a workflow may still prescribe which sources to consult and which checks to run. If the chosen sources lack relevant evidence, even accurate extraction can leave a financial question unanswered. LLM agents can adapt the workflow as evidence emerges. They use the graph and earlier findings to decide where to look next, which claims to verify, and whether to update a record for later use. This is the first survey devoted to how LLM agents reshape the construction, maintenance, and use of financial KGs. Our taxonomy covers Knowledge Graph Construction, Temporal Evolution, Verification, Reconciliation, and Admission, Adaptive Acquisition, and Knowledge Graph Usage. We examine how studies evaluate graph quality, agents' use of evidence, financial task outcomes, and reliability over time. These evaluations show that agents can recover evidence missed in an initial search and revise records as new information arrives. Three questions remain unresolved. How can an agent tell whether it has enough evidence for a financial decision? After a record is corrected, how can the agent identify which earlier conclusions need to change? Which relationships and rules can it reuse in a new graph or domain?

The llama.cpp × AMD Benchmark dashboard is available on Hugging Face. It lets you track prompt processing and text generation performance across llama.cpp builds, models, and quantizations, so you can explore how local inference performs on AMD Ryzen and Radeon hardware.

Local inference performance changes as models, kernels, and builds evolve. We want those changes to be easy to inspect for any AMD developer: pick a hardware, a model and a build, compare quantizations, and follow performance over time. The benchmark workflow and underlying results are public, so you can also inspect how we benchmark inference performance.

You can choose Hardware, Model, and llama.cpp build in the Configuration sidebar. The current hardware choices are Radeon 8060S (gfx1151) and Radeon AI Pro R9700S (gfx1201).

The dashboard shows two separate tests, both measured in tokens per second:.

Sources indicate that both tests start at context depth zero (n_depth=0). PP512 measures processing 512 input tokens without generation; TG128 measures generating 128 tokens without a pre-existing context. The plotted value is the mean throughput (avg_ts). These are useful reference workloads, while the Context scaling tab lets you explore token generation throughput as the context grows.

We benchmark the prebuilt binaries distributed through llama-install.sh, the build and installation project behind llama.app. The public gfx1151 and gfx1201 workflows are scheduled weekly and run the standard benchmarks using the llama-bench tool with Flash Attention on and off, with 10 repetitions per configuration.

In a recent development, the model set evolves and presently includes Inkling 2 Mini, Qwen, Gemma, gpt-oss, and LFM models, covering both dense and mixture-of-experts architectures. Available GGUF formats include Q4_K_M, Q8_0, other quantizations, and higher-precision formats such as BF16 and F16.

In a recent development, the explorer reads directly from the public ggml-org/install.sh-benches-data Storage Bucket on Hugging Face. The data source link beside the chart title opens the folder for the selected build, hardware, and model.

It has been revealed that standard results use ///.jsonl. Workload sweeps use the same folder -tg.jsonl filename.

Use them to investigate a result, make your own charts, or compare with a local run.

It has been revealed that thanks to the AMD team for providing test infrastructure and helping validate the setup! Try the dashboard, inspect the data, and let us know which models and workloads you would like to see next.

If you used the ParkMobile app to pay for parking at a meter several years ago, you might be getting a payment as a result of a data breach. Unfortunately, it’s probably not an amount you’d expect for the inconvenience of having your data exposed. And while it’s a comically low amount, don’t spend it all in one place, because, well…. You’re literally not allowed to.

Here’s what’s happening and why the ParkMobile data beach settlement is raising eyebrows online.

Also: Hackers stole 1 billion records from Salesforce customer databases with this simple trick – don’t fall for it.

According to recent reports, in 2021, hackers accessed sensitive data from more than 21 million ParkMobile customers, including license plate numbers, email addresses, phone numbers, and mailing addresses. The hackers didn’t get any payment information.

ParkMobile denied any wrongdoing but agreed to a settlement to avoid the cost and time of going to court. If you filed a claim, you could choose to get your payment in cash — up to $25. If you didn’t file a claim but you were still affected, you probably received an email this week with your alternative payment — $1.

“As part of the agreed resolution,” the email explained, “you are entitled to receive a benefit.” The email went on to say that the benefit is a $1 discount code for the ParkMobile app.

Recent findings suggest that first, the payment is only good for credit towards ParkMobile service fees (not even the actual parking fee), so you have to park at a ParkMobile-owned lot to use your benefit. Second, you have to enter the code you received manually in your account. Third, you can’t use your $1 all at once.

Sources indicate that your code is good for 25 cents off a ParkMobile service fee, the email explained, and it can be used up to four times, equaling $1. When I searched a few ParkMobile lots near me, service fees were between $1.80 and $4.

Get the biggest stories in tech every Friday with ZDNET’s Week in Review newsletter.

Sources indicate that naturally, users who received the email were quick to criticize. Several Reddit posts appeared, with users pointing out that you had to pay significantly more than your benefit to actually use it, claiming the settlement was just a ploy for lawyers to get paid, and some saying they thought the email was a phishing attempt.

Customers who received a $1 code have one year to use it.

#38216. The Information Content of News Embeddings

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (224 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

The Information Content of News Embeddings

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (224 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.33458v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Does the predictive success of news embeddings reflect a better measure of news surprises or other sources of return predictability in text? We decompose news embeddings by content into event-category, firm-identity, and idiosyncratic components, and by timing into historical levels and current deviations. At short horizons, event categories account for most of the predictive power of embedding forecasts, and simple forecasts based on historical average returns after news in each event category outperform them. At longer horizons, firm information already present in earlier news coverage accounts for a substantial share of return predictability, even after residualization on firm characteristics. The dominance of event categories persists, and historical levels still contribute in the first months, when using a language model pretrained entirely before our sample period. For Llama-2, even embeddings constructed from news more than three years old predict returns at long horizons. However, its predictive advantage over RoBERTa is concentrated in firm identity and the historical level, and its advantage in these components largely disappears by its pretraining cutoff. A calibration shows that pretraining memory, a source of look-ahead bias, can account for this pattern. Describing news more fully is not the same as measuring news surprises, and persistent return predictability from news text does not by itself establish slow incorporation of news into prices.

  • Discovery is available through the new API Gateway API Portal, which recognizes the AI endpoints among the APIs it discovers automatically from traffic logs and service configuration records, with no agents to deploy or logs to forward.
